topic: Frontier Lab · Phase 3: Empirical Scaling (Addition Transformer)

questions.title: Designing an IsoFLOP matrix
questions.prompt: You're deriving your own scaling law for the addition transformer. Design an IsoFLOP experiment matrix: vary model size N from ~1M to ~15M params, vary tokens D at each fixed compute budget C=6ND, and explain how you'd read off the compute-optimal frontier.
probes: Why fix C and sweep N (with D implied) rather than sweeping N and D independently?
How many N points and C budgets do you need before the fitted frontier is trustworthy?
criteria: C=6ND relation
fix C, sweep N, derive D=C/6N
loss vs N parabola per IsoFLOP curve
minimum of each curve gives N_opt(C)
enough C budgets to fit a trend, not just one point

no_hire.answer: I'd just train a few different sized models and see which one has the lowest loss.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No compute accounting, no notion of holding C fixed, no frontier concept. Can't operationalize the experiment.

weak_hire.answer: Pick several model sizes N, train each for some number of steps, and plot loss vs N. The best one is compute-optimal. I'd also vary the number of tokens D somewhat.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: No explicit use of C=6ND, no fixed-compute discipline across a curve, so N and D are confounded and the result isn't a real frontier.

hire.answer: Use C=6ND. For each compute budget C, sweep several N values from 1M to 15M and compute D=C/(6N) for each, so every point on that curve costs the same FLOPs. Plot loss vs N for that C -- it's a parabola; its minimum is N_opt(C). Repeat for several C budgets (e.g. 3-5x apart) to get several (C, N_opt) pairs, then fit N_opt ∝ C^a to read the scaling exponent.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct mechanics: fixed-C sweep, per-curve minimum, multiple budgets to fit a trend. Missing discussion of how many points/budgets are enough for a reliable fit and what could go wrong with a small param range.

strong_hire.answer: IsoFLOP: for each of several C budgets, sweep N over 1M-15M (say 6-8 log-spaced points) and set D=C/(6N) so every run in that curve costs the same FLOPs; plot final loss vs log N -- it's convex, and its minimum gives N_opt(C). I need at least 4-5 well-separated C budgets (each ~2-3x apart) so the resulting N_opt(C) points span enough of a log-log range to fit a reliable power law N_opt ∝ C^a; too few budgets or too narrow an N range lets me fit any exponent to noise. At small scale I'd also watch for: curves that don't show a clean minimum within my N range (need to extend it), high run-to-run variance at small N/D requiring multiple seeds, and the fact that 6ND is an approximation ignoring embedding/vocab FLOPs which matters more at these tiny sizes. I'd log all (N, D, C, loss) tuples so the same data also supports fitting D_opt(C) and the joint loss law in question 5, rather than re-running.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Names the log-spacing and budget-separation requirements for a trustworthy fit, flags small-scale noise and the 6ND approximation's breakdown at tiny N, and connects the design to reuse for downstream curve fitting. Staff-level experimental design.

questions.title: Single-batch overfit before real training
questions.prompt: Before launching any real training run on the addition transformer, you overfit a single batch to near-zero loss. Why is this step non-negotiable, and what exactly does it verify that a normal training curve wouldn't catch early?
probes: What specific bugs does this catch that a slowly-decreasing loss on the full dataset would mask?
What loss value and how many steps would make you suspicious even if loss is decreasing?
criteria: isolates gradient flow / plumbing from data/generalization issues
near-zero loss is achievable if capacity > data in the batch
catches label leakage, wrong masking, frozen params, wrong loss reduction
cheap and fast -- fails in seconds not hours
distinguishes optimization bugs from real underfitting later

no_hire.answer: It's a sanity check to make sure the code runs without errors.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Doesn't understand what's actually being verified beyond 'no crash'. Would miss silent bugs like a detached gradient or wrong target shift.

weak_hire.answer: If the model can't memorize a tiny batch, something is broken in the model or training loop. It's a quick way to catch bugs before spending compute on a real run.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct high-level purpose, but no specifics on which classes of bug this isolates or why near-zero loss specifically is the bar, not just 'lower loss'.

hire.answer: With enough capacity relative to one batch, the model should drive loss to near-zero within a few hundred steps -- if it can't, gradients aren't flowing correctly somewhere (frozen layer, wrong optimizer target, loss computed on the wrong tensor, or a masking bug that hides the label). This isolates plumbing correctness from data quality and generalization, which a full run can't do because a slowly-decreasing full-dataset loss looks superficially healthy even with a real bug underneath. It's also cheap: minutes instead of hours, so you fail fast.
hire.interviewer_note: Names the mechanism (capacity > data implies near-zero achievable) and gives concrete bug classes it catches. Missing the specific failure signature that would make you suspicious mid-run.

strong_hire.answer: The test isolates the gradient-flow-correctness question from the generalization question. With model capacity far exceeding a single batch's information content, loss should approach zero (bounded below by numerical floor, not by any real underfitting) within a few hundred to low-thousand steps; failure to do so means the loop is broken, not that the task is hard. It catches bugs a slow full-dataset loss curve masks entirely: off-by-one label shift (model still 'learns' something from shifted targets, producing plausible-looking but wrong loss curves), a masking bug that leaks the answer into the input, frozen or untied parameters, wrong reduction (mean vs sum) silently changing effective learning rate, or gradients not reaching an embedding table due to an indexing bug. Concretely for the addition transformer I'd overfit one batch of, say, 4-16 examples and expect loss under 1e-3 within a couple hundred steps on a model with a few hundred thousand+ params; if loss plateaus above that or decreases but plateaus at a suspicious value like exactly the loss of predicting the most common digit, that's a signature of a specific bug (usually target misalignment) rather than 'needs more steps'. I keep this as a permanent pytest-style regression check, not a one-off, since any refactor of the data pipeline or loss can silently reintroduce these bugs.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Distinguishes gradient-flow correctness from generalization explicitly, gives a concrete quantitative bar and diagnostic signatures (e.g. plateau at most-common-digit loss implying target misalignment), and treats it as a permanent regression test rather than a one-time step. Staff-level production discipline.

questions.title: Static shapes and JIT recompilation storms
questions.prompt: Your JAX training loop keeps stalling for seconds at a time with no obvious error. You suspect it's XLA recompiling. Explain the mechanism and how deterministic padding fixes it.
probes: Why does JAX recompile at all -- what's it doing differently from eager PyTorch?
If padding solves shape variation, what other source of retracing could still bite you?
criteria: jax.jit traces per unique input shape/dtype/static-arg signature
variable-length sequences produce a new shape each batch
each new shape triggers a fresh XLA compile, which is expensive
fixed padding to a max length gives one stable shape, compiled once
other retrace triggers: python control flow on traced values, changing static args, donated buffers

no_hire.answer: JAX is just slower sometimes, maybe it's a GPU issue or I need a bigger batch size.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No understanding of JIT tracing at all. Wouldn't be able to diagnose or fix this in practice.

weak_hire.answer: jax.jit compiles the function the first time it's called, and recompiles if the input shape changes. If my addition examples have different digit lengths, each batch might have a different shape, causing recompiles. Padding all sequences to the same length avoids this.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct mechanism and correct fix, but doesn't explain why recompilation is expensive or why it manifests as intermittent stalls rather than a one-time cost.

hire.answer: jax.jit traces the function into an XLA computation graph keyed by the abstract shape/dtype signature of its inputs (and any static args); a new signature triggers a full retrace and XLA compile, which can take seconds to tens of seconds -- far more than one training step. If addition problems have variable digit counts and I don't pad, nearly every batch has a different sequence length, so I pay a compile every step, which looks like random stalls. Fix: pad every example to one fixed maximum sequence length (and pad the batch dimension too if it varies) so the shape signature is constant across the whole run, and XLA compiles exactly once.
hire.interviewer_note: Explains the compile-per-signature mechanism and connects it to the specific symptom (stalls = compiles). Doesn't mention other latent retrace triggers beyond sequence length, e.g. changing static args or Python-level branching.

strong_hire.answer: jax.jit lazily traces your function into an XLA HLO graph the first time it sees a given (shape, dtype, static-argument) signature, caches the compiled executable keyed on that signature, and reuses it on subsequent calls with the same signature; a new signature is a cache miss and forces a fresh trace-and-compile, which is O(seconds) versus O(milliseconds) for a cached dispatch -- exactly the intermittent multi-second stalls you're seeing. For the addition transformer, variable operand digit counts mean variable sequence length per batch unless you pad, so essentially every batch is a cache miss: a 'recompilation storm'. The fix is deterministic padding -- pad inputs and targets to one fixed max length (covering your largest supported operand size with margin) and pad the batch to a fixed size too (drop or pad the final partial batch) so exactly one shape signature exists for the whole run, giving exactly one compile. Beyond padding, other latent retrace triggers to guard against: passing hyperparameters as Python ints/floats that vary run to run when they're static_argnums, using Python control flow (if/for) on traced values instead of lax.cond/lax.scan, and donate_argnums mismatches. In production I'd assert on the compiled-function cache size (jax's internal cache, or wrapping with a compile counter) in CI so a future PR that reintroduces variable shapes fails loudly instead of silently degrading throughput 10-100x.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Full trace-cache mechanism with the cost asymmetry, correctly attributes stalls as compile-cache misses, gives the concrete fix including batch-dimension padding, and lists additional retrace triggers plus a CI guardrail to prevent regression. Staff-level systems understanding of JAX internals.

questions.title: Strict exact-match eval vs teacher-forced loss
questions.prompt: Your addition transformer has low teacher-forced validation loss, but you're not confident it can actually add. Explain why teacher-forced loss overstates true capability, and what a strict eval should measure instead.
probes: Concretely, at inference time what's different about how the model sees its own previous digit?
If the model gets digit 3 of 6 wrong during autoregressive generation, what happens to digits 4-6, and does teacher-forcing ever expose that?
criteria: teacher forcing feeds ground-truth previous tokens regardless of model's own prediction
real inference is autoregressive: errors compound because wrong tokens feed forward
exposure bias -- train/eval-time mismatch
strict eval: greedy/sampled autoregressive decode, exact match on the full digit sequence
single wrong digit should fail the whole example, not be averaged away

no_hire.answer: Validation loss already tells you how good the model is, so if it's low the model is working.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Doesn't understand the distinction between teacher-forced and autoregressive evaluation at all. Would ship a broken model believing it works.

weak_hire.answer: Teacher forcing gives the model the correct previous tokens even if it made a mistake, so the loss looks better than real generation would be. A stricter eval should have the model generate its own tokens step by step and check if the final answer is correct.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correctly identifies the mismatch and proposes autoregressive eval, but doesn't explain the compounding-error mechanism or why per-digit averaging in loss hides total failures.

hire.answer: Teacher-forced loss conditions each predicted position on the ground-truth prefix, so even if the model would have derailed after getting digit 3 wrong, teacher forcing resets it to the correct context at digit 4 -- this is exposure bias, a train/eval mismatch with real autoregressive inference where the model conditions on its own (possibly wrong) previous output and errors compound. Also, loss is averaged per-token across the sequence, so one wrong digit in an otherwise correct 6-digit answer barely moves the average loss, while the actual answer is completely wrong. The strict eval: run the model autoregressively (greedy decode) with no ground-truth feeding, and score exact match on the entire output sequence -- one wrong digit fails the whole example.
hire.interviewer_note: Correctly explains exposure bias and the per-token-averaging masking effect, and specifies the right strict metric. Missing discussion of how large the loss-vs-exact-match gap can get in practice or how to diagnose which digit positions fail most.

strong_hire.answer: Teacher-forced loss is computed with every position conditioned on the true prefix regardless of the model's own prediction at prior steps -- this is exposure bias: the model never has to recover from its own mistakes during training or in this eval mode, so a model that's fragile to compounding errors can still show low, smoothly-decreasing per-token loss. Two things hide the real failure rate: first, per-token cross-entropy is averaged, so a model correct on 5 of 6 output digits gets ~83% of positions right and a deceptively low loss, even though the numeric answer is 100% wrong; second, teacher forcing always re-anchors the model to ground truth at the next step, so it never exposes what happens when a wrong digit 3 changes the input to the model's own digit-4 prediction -- in free-running generation that one error can cascade (e.g. carry propagation errors are especially bad for addition, since a wrong digit changes the carry the model needs for every subsequent digit). The honest eval is full autoregressive decoding: seed with only the input, let the model generate every output digit conditioned on its own previous outputs, and score strict exact-match on the complete answer string (plus EOS placement) -- not a per-token or per-position accuracy, since partial credit doesn't correspond to a correct sum. I'd also report per-digit-position accuracy under autoregressive decoding (not teacher-forced) to see if errors concentrate at specific positions (e.g. carries into the most significant digit), and track the gap between teacher-forced loss and exact-match rate over training as a canary -- a widening gap signals the model is learning to exploit teacher forcing rather than the actual addition algorithm.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Names exposure bias precisely, explains carry-propagation as the addition-specific compounding mechanism, insists on whole-string exact match rather than partial credit, and proposes tracking the teacher-forced/exact-match gap as an ongoing diagnostic. Staff-level rigor connecting the general ML failure mode to the specific task structure.

questions.title: Fitting the power law with curve_fit
questions.prompt: You have loss values from your IsoFLOP runs. Walk through how you'd fit a scaling law with scipy's curve_fit, and how you'd interpret the resulting exponents to know if your setup actually follows a power law.
probes: Why fit in log-log space or with a log-loss objective rather than raw loss with least squares?
What would a poor fit (bad residuals, wildly unstable exponent under resampling) actually tell you about your experiment?
criteria: parametric form L(N) or L(N,D) with irreducible loss term
fit in log space to avoid domination by large-loss outliers / heteroscedasticity
curve_fit needs reasonable initial guesses and bounds for these nonlinear params
read the exponent (power) as the interpretable scaling rate, compare across N and D
sanity-check fit quality: residuals, refit stability, not just R^2

no_hire.answer: I'd plot loss against N and D and eyeball a trend line.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No actual curve fitting, no functional form, no exponent, no way to make a quantitative claim.

weak_hire.answer: I'd fit something like L = a*N^(-b) using scipy.optimize.curve_fit and look at the fitted b as the scaling exponent. A good fit means the power law holds.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Right general shape and tool, but omits the irreducible loss floor, doesn't mention log-space fitting or initial guesses, and 'good fit' isn't defined.

hire.answer: I'd fit L(N) = L_inf + a*N^(-alpha), since real losses have an irreducible floor (entropy of the task, or here, guessing floor). curve_fit is nonlinear least squares so I need sensible initial guesses (e.g. L_inf near my best observed loss, alpha near 0.3-0.5 as a prior from published laws) and bounds so it doesn't diverge. I'd fit in log(L - L_inf) space or at least weight residuals in log space, since loss differences at small N are huge and would dominate a raw least-squares fit and swamp the informative differences at large N. The fitted alpha is the scaling rate -- I'd report it with its confidence interval and check the fit visually on a log-log plot before trusting it.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct functional form with irreducible term, correct reasoning for log-space fitting, and mentions initial guesses/bounds and CI. Missing a concrete stability check like refitting on subsamples or bootstrapping the exponent.

strong_hire.answer: Functional form: L(N) = L_inf + a*N^(-alpha) for the N-only IsoFLOP-minimum fit, or the joint Chinchilla-style L(N,D) = L_inf + a/N^alpha + b/D^beta for the full grid, since a bare power law with no floor will misfit at large N/D where loss is approaching an irreducible level (task entropy plus optimization noise floor). Because curve_fit does nonlinear least squares and this surface can have multiple local minima, I give it informed initial guesses (L_inf slightly below my lowest observed loss, alpha/beta around 0.3-0.5 as priors from Chinchilla-style results, though my exponents may differ since addition is a much narrower task) and bounds to keep parameters in a sane range so the optimizer doesn't diverge to a degenerate fit like alpha near 0. Critically, I fit on log-transformed residuals (or at minimum use weighted least squares downweighting large-loss points) because raw squared error in loss space is dominated by the biggest losses at small N, which are the least interesting points -- I want the fit driven by the informative curvature near the frontier, not by how bad my smallest model is. To trust the exponent I don't just look at R^2: I bootstrap-resample the (N, loss) points and refit repeatedly to get a confidence interval on alpha, and I check that residuals are unstructured on the log-log plot rather than showing curvature, which would indicate the wrong functional form (e.g. missing the irreducible term, or a regime change where a single power law doesn't hold across my whole N range). A wildly unstable alpha under resampling, or a fit that only 'works' because of one or two extreme points, tells me either I don't have enough distinct compute budgets, my measured losses are too noisy (need multiple seeds per point), or the task's true scaling behavior isn't a clean single power law at this scale -- all of which are honest, reportable findings, not fitting failures to hide.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Full joint functional form with irreducible term for both N and D, explicit reasoning about optimizer local minima and log-space weighting, and a genuine model-diagnosis process using bootstrap CIs and residual structure rather than trusting a point estimate. Treats an unstable fit as a real experimental finding. Staff/research-lead rigor.

questions.title: Dense vs MoE scaling frontier comparison
questions.prompt: You repeat the IsoFLOP sweep with a Mixture-of-Experts version of the addition transformer at matched active-parameter compute. What differences do you expect in the resulting scaling frontier, and specifically why would MoE be more data-hungry per active parameter?
probes: If dense and MoE match on active FLOPs/token, what's the actual axis MoE is spending extra budget on, and how does that show up in the D-vs-N tradeoff?
At the tiny scale of this crucible (millions of params, synthetic addition data), would you expect the MoE data-hunger effect to even be visible, or does it only emerge at larger scale?
criteria: MoE decouples total params from active FLOPs/token, C=6ND uses active N so total capacity is larger for same C
each expert sees fewer effective tokens per param than a dense model of matched active size, since routing splits tokens across experts
expect MoE optimal D/N ratio to shift -- needs relatively more tokens (or more total training) per active param to reach the same loss as dense
load-balancing / routing noise adds an extra source of sample inefficiency vs dense at small scale
at this tiny scale, effect may be dominated by noise / too few experts to see a clean signal -- caution about overclaiming

no_hire.answer: MoE has more total parameters so it should just be better than dense at the same compute.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No understanding of active vs total params, no mechanism for why MoE would need more data, and doesn't even engage with the actual experimental prediction being asked for.

weak_hire.answer: MoE only activates some experts per token, so it's compute-cheap but has more total parameters to train, meaning each expert gets less data per parameter. I'd expect MoE to need more tokens than dense to reach the same loss.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: States the right conclusion and a rough intuition, but doesn't explain the C=6ND accounting (which N is being matched) or connect it to the specific IsoFLOP experiment being run, and gives no caveat about scale.

hire.answer: C=6ND is computed on active parameters, so a MoE model matched to a dense model on active N (and thus on C) has many more total parameters spread across experts. Since routing sends each token to only top-k of E experts, an individual expert effectively sees a fraction of the training tokens, so for the same active-parameter count and the same D, each expert is more data-starved than the single dense FFN would be. I'd expect the MoE IsoFLOP curves to have their loss-minimizing D/N point shifted toward needing more tokens per active param than dense, i.e. MoE compute-optimal frontier is more data-hungry. At this small scale with limited synthetic data, I'd also expect load-balancing noise to add variance to the MoE curves that dense doesn't have.
hire.interviewer_note: Correctly explains the active-vs-total accounting and per-expert data dilution, and predicts the D/N shift plus extra small-scale noise. Missing an explicit caution about whether this effect is even resolvable given the tiny model/data scale in this specific crucible.

strong_hire.answer: C=6ND is conventionally computed on active parameters per token, so matching a MoE model to a dense model on active N holds C fixed while the MoE model carries E times (or top-k/E fraction) more total parameters distributed across experts. The mechanism for extra data-hunger: routing partitions the token stream, so each expert only receives roughly D/E_eff tokens (E_eff being the effective number of experts it competes with under the router's load distribution) rather than the full D that a dense FFN of the same active size would see -- each expert is a smaller effective model trained on a smaller effective slice of data, which is exactly the low-D, high-underfitting regime of the same power law, just applied per-expert. I'd predict the MoE IsoFLOP curves' minima sit at a higher D/N_active ratio than dense's, meaning the MoE compute-optimal point wants relatively more tokens (or, equivalently, at fixed D, MoE needs more compute/N_active to close the gap) -- this matches the qualitative real-world finding that MoE needs careful token-per-expert accounting and tends to be more sample-hungry at small-to-moderate token budgets, closing the gap only once each expert has seen enough tokens to specialize usefully. At this crucible's scale (single-digit millions of active params, small E, purely synthetic uniform-distribution addition data), I'd be cautious about overclaiming: with few experts and a narrow, uniform task, routing may barely specialize at all (experts could look nearly identical, effectively acting like a slightly-regularized dense ensemble), so the classic data-hunger gap might be muted or swamped by run-to-run noise -- I'd want to check the router's entropy/load-balance stats and confirm experts are actually differentiating before trusting any exponent difference between the dense and MoE fitted curves, otherwise I'm fitting noise and calling it a scaling law difference.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Precise mechanism connecting per-expert token dilution back to the same underlying power law applied at the expert level, correct directional prediction on the D/N shift, and a genuinely staff-level caveat that at this specific tiny scale the effect may not even be observable without checking routing entropy/load-balance diagnostics first. Avoids overclaiming from a small experiment -- exactly the instinct that separates research rigor from pattern-matching a known result.
